prompt: In the DMBOK's terms, choosing that CPFs are kept only as ciphertext was governance. What was lesson 5's `ALTER TABLE`?
hint: One decides, the other carries out.

choices.text: Management
choices.why: Right. Management carries out what governance decided.

choices.text: Governance as well, since it changed the data
choices.why: No. Changing the data is carrying out the decision.

choices.text: Architecture
choices.why: No. Architecture is another DMBOK area, about structures.

choices.text: An audit
choices.why: No. An audit checks; it does not change anything.

prompt: Why does this course keep each governance decision in a table rather than a wiki page?
hint: What can be done with rows?

choices.text: Tables are faster to read than pages
choices.why: No. Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: The LGPD forbids keeping decisions in documents
choices.why: No. It asks for accountability, not a format.

choices.text: A row answers to a query, a test and an audit
choices.why: Right. A wiki page can only be believed.

choices.text: Wikis cannot hold tables
choices.why: No. They can; they just do not stay true.

prompt: A governance programme makes every new column wait three weeks for a committee. What does the lesson expect to happen?
hint: Where does the data go instead?

choices.text: Data quality improves, since every column is reviewed
choices.why: No. Review that slow drives the data elsewhere.

choices.text: Fewer columns are created, which is the aim
choices.why: No. The aim is good decisions, not fewer columns.

choices.text: The committee becomes the owner of every table
choices.why: No. Ownership is not what a committee gains this way.

choices.text: People keep data where the committee cannot see it
choices.why: Right. A spreadsheet or a private bucket, governed worse than before.

prompt: Match each role to what it answers for.

pairs.right: what the data is for and who may use it
whether it is correct and documented
where it is stored and secured

prompt: Why is a table's owner a role, like "head of sales", and not a person's name?

choices.text: Names are personal data and must not be stored
choices.why: No. The steward column holds names, classified as personal.

choices.text: A person changes jobs; the role stays
choices.why: Right. A table owned by a name is owned by nobody once that person leaves.

choices.text: Roles have more privileges than people
choices.why: No. Ownership here is about answering, not privileges.

choices.text: Only roles can own tables in PostgreSQL
choices.why: No. That is the database owner, a different thing.

prompt: How many tables did `unowned.sql` list?
Which table on the unowned list is the most common finding of a first inventory?

choices.text: `gov.table_owners`, the ownership table itself
choices.why: Right. The table that records ownership had none.

choices.text: `sales.returns`, created to show a privilege
choices.why: No. A real finding, but not the one the lesson singles out.

choices.text: `gov.holidays`, which needs next year's rows
choices.why: No. It needs an owner, but it is not the one meant.

choices.text: `support.agent_regions`, used by row security
choices.why: No. It is unowned too, but not the one meant.

prompt: Match each defect at Ipê to its quality dimension.

pairs.left: the same customer signed up twice
a payment that differs from its order
an address the customer moved from

prompt: Which dimension cannot be measured with SQL alone?

choices.text: Uniqueness
choices.why: No. A GROUP BY measures it.

choices.text: Completeness
choices.why: No. Counting nulls measures it.

choices.text: Accuracy
choices.why: Right. It needs something outside the database, such as a sample.

choices.text: Validity
choices.why: No. A pattern or a range measures it.

prompt: Why is a duplicate customer a privacy problem as well as a business one?

choices.text: It doubles the person's consent
choices.why: No. Consent is per act, not per row.

choices.text: Duplicated rows always count as sensitive data under the LGPD
choices.why: No. The class does not change with the count.

choices.text: The LGPD caps how many rows a person may have
choices.why: No. There is no such cap.

choices.text: An access or erasure request finds only half of the person
choices.why: Right. The other account is left out, or left behind.

prompt: How many e-mail addresses failed the shape check?
hint: The first row of the measurement.

prompt: Seven addresses end in `.con`. Why did the shape check pass them?

choices.text: The regular expression treats upper and lower case as different letters
choices.why: No. It uses `~*`, which ignores case.

choices.text: Their shape is valid; only the domain is wrong
choices.why: Right. A rule about shape cannot see a typo that keeps the shape.

choices.text: `.con` is a real top-level domain
choices.why: No. It does not exist; that is the problem.

choices.text: The check skips every customer who was created before the year 2020
choices.why: No. It has no date condition.

prompt: Why are the 14 orders with no customer not a defect?

choices.text: They are 2019 guest checkouts, which the old site allowed
choices.why: Right. A record of how the business worked then.

choices.text: They were cancelled, so the customer was removed
choices.why: No. Their dates explain them, not their status.

choices.text: Their customers asked to be erased
choices.why: No. Erasure kept the customer row in lesson 7.

choices.text: Nulls are never defects
choices.why: No. A null since 2020 would be one.

prompt: What do all 8 consents recorded on a different day from sign-up have in common?

choices.text: They were all given by minors
choices.why: No. The query says nothing about age.

choices.text: They were all withdrawn later on, through the unsubscribe link in an e-mail
choices.why: No. Withdrawal is in the event log, not in this query.

choices.text: They are all duplicate customers, given the first account's consent
choices.why: Right. Explained, and wrong: a consent belongs to the act of giving it.

choices.text: They all came from the shop counter
choices.why: No. The channel is not in this query.

prompt: 1,316 consents fall on the sign-up day, hours before the account. What can the database say about why?
hint: It can point; it cannot explain.

choices.text: That customers consented in the shop before signing up online
choices.why: No. Nothing in the data shows that.

choices.text: That the consents are forged
choices.why: No. A same-day gap is not evidence of forgery.

choices.text: That PostgreSQL stored the times in the wrong time zone
choices.why: No. Nothing points at the database itself.

choices.text: Only where to ask: whoever built the sign-up form
choices.why: Right. The date agrees and the time does not; the form knows why.

prompt: Put the life of a quality finding in order.
hint: Nobody changes data before the owner decides.
items: Look at the rows behind the count
Fix it where the data is made
Keep a rule that runs every day

prompt: Why does Ipê not delete one row of each duplicate pair?
hint: What points at a customer row?

choices.text: The LGPD forbids deleting customers
choices.why: No. It asks for deletion in some cases.

choices.text: Orders, prescriptions and requests point at both
choices.why: Right. Deleting one breaks what points at it.

choices.text: Duplicates are kept on purpose so that the quality rules have something to measure
choices.why: No. Measuring is not a reason to keep a defect.

choices.text: Nobody can tell which of the two accounts is the newer one of the pair
choices.why: No. `created_at` says which is newer.

prompt: Why does the guest-order rule ask about nulls since 2020 instead of any null?

choices.text: A rule should fail only on something somebody has to act on
choices.why: Right. Fourteen correct rows would make it fail forever.

choices.text: Queries that reach back over several years of old data are far too slow
choices.why: No. Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Orders before 2020 have been deleted
choices.why: No. They are still there.

choices.text: The LGPD does not apply before 2020
choices.why: No. It has applied since 2020 to all data held, whatever its age.

prompt: What does `gov.quality_runs` let Ipê say that today's numbers alone cannot?

choices.text: Which customer broke each rule
choices.why: No. It stores counts, not customers.

choices.text: How long each rule took to run
choices.why: No. It does not record time taken.

choices.text: Whether each problem is getting better or worse
choices.why: Right. And that it is monitored, for accountability.

choices.text: Which rules to delete
choices.why: No. The reason column helps with that, not the history.

prompt: Each rule in `gov.quality_rules` has a ___ of zero: how many rows may break it and still pass.
What does `NOT VALID` do to the `email_shape` constraint?

choices.text: It disables the constraint until it is validated
choices.why: No. New rows are refused at once.

choices.text: It deletes the rows that break it
choices.why: No. It never touches existing rows.

choices.text: It turns the constraint into a warning
choices.why: No. A refused insert is an error, not a warning.

choices.text: New rows are checked; existing ones are not, until VALIDATE
choices.why: Right. Stop the bleeding now, fix the old rows later.

prompt: Put the three steps of section 8 in order.
items: Fix the old rows at the owner's pace

prompt: Why can a `CHECK` constraint not refuse orders dated in the future?

choices.text: Timestamps cannot appear in a CHECK
choices.why: No. They can; comparing with a fixed date is fine.

choices.text: A CHECK must not depend on the current date, and `now()` does
choices.why: Right. A trigger, or the import, has to do it.

choices.text: Future dates are valid in PostgreSQL
choices.why: No. That is true and does not explain it.

choices.text: The constraint would be too slow on large tables
choices.why: No. Speed is not the problem.

prompt: Match each kind of metadata to an example from the lesson.
What does a data dictionary generated from the database show that a hand-written one hides?

choices.text: Its own gaps: columns nobody has described yet
choices.why: Right. A hand-written one just leaves them out.

choices.text: The data in each column
choices.why: No. A dictionary describes columns, not their values.

choices.text: Who changed each column last
choices.why: No. That is not in the catalogue.

choices.text: The cost of each column in storage
choices.why: No. The query does not read sizes.

prompt: How many view-to-table edges did `lineage.sql` find?
How does PostgreSQL know which tables a view reads?

choices.text: From the query log
choices.why: No. The dependency is recorded when the view is created.

choices.text: The view's owner declares it in a comment
choices.why: No. Nobody has to declare it.

choices.text: It records the dependency, to refuse dropping a table a view needs
choices.why: Right. In `pg_depend`, through the view's rewrite rule.

choices.text: It parses the SQL text of every view again, each time somebody asks it
choices.why: No. It stores the dependency instead.

prompt: Which edges of Ipê's lineage map does no tool see unless somebody declares them?

choices.text: The ones from tables to views
choices.why: No. The database records those.

choices.text: The ones between two views that read each other inside the database
choices.why: No. Those are in `pg_depend` too.

choices.text: Foreign keys between tables
choices.why: No. The catalogue has those.

choices.text: Copies outside the database: extracts, backups, AI systems
choices.why: Right. Exactly where an erasure misses.

prompt: Match each tool of this lesson to the question it answers.

pairs.right: what breaks if I change this?

prompt: An analyst finds 3 orders dated 2027 and corrects the dates by hand. What is still wrong?

choices.text: Nothing; the three rows are now right
choices.why: No. The import will write the next one.

choices.text: The import that wrote them is unchanged, and the owner was not asked
choices.why: Right. Fix at the source, after the owner decides.

choices.text: Hand corrections are forbidden by the LGPD
choices.why: No. The law says nothing of the sort.

choices.text: The rule in `gov.quality_rules` must now be deleted
choices.why: No. The rule keeps watching for the next one.
